scarcity-s1.title: One empty lot in Riverton
scarcity-s1.text: The town of Riverton (an invented town) owns one empty lot downtown. Residents want a park, store owners want a parking garage, and a grocery chain offers to lease the lot for a new store. Building the garage would take a crew of 40 construction workers, two cranes and a fleet of dump trucks, and a local developer has offered to put up her own savings to run the project.

table.caption: Who answers the basic economic questions in three invented countries
rows: Households and firms, through buying and selling
By buyers and sellers in markets
Mostly households and firms; the government runs schools and roads
Mostly in markets, with some government rules

items.q: What makes the choice about Riverton's lot an economic problem?
options: The town has run out of money for any project
The lot cannot be used for a park, a garage and a store at the same time
Store owners care more than residents do
The grocery chain sets the price of the lease

why.correct: Scarcity: one limited resource and several wants for it, so the town must choose.
options: The scenario says nothing about the budget; even a rich town faces the choice.
Right: limited land, unlimited wants for it, so a choice must be made.
How much each group cares does not create the problem; the limited lot does.
The lease price matters for the choice but does not create the scarcity.

items.q: Which factor of production is the lot itself?
options: Land
Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship

why.correct: Land means natural resources and the ground itself.
options: Right: the lot is a natural resource.
Labor is human effort, such as the construction crew.
Capital is made tools and buildings, such as the cranes.
Entrepreneurship is the organizing and risk-taking of the developer.

items.q: In the garage plan, which item is capital?
options: The 40 construction workers
The empty lot
The developer's willingness to risk her savings
The two cranes and the dump trucks

why.correct: Capital is goods made to produce other goods: machines, tools, buildings.
options: Workers supply labor.
The lot is land.
Taking the risk and organizing the project is entrepreneurship.
Right: cranes and trucks are made tools used in production.

items.q: The developer offers her own savings to run the garage project. Which factor of production does she supply, and why?
options: Capital, because she provides money
Labor, because she works on the project
Entrepreneurship, because she organizes the project and takes the risk
Land, because the garage sits on the lot

why.correct: Entrepreneurship combines the other factors and bears the risk. Money by itself is not a factor; it buys factors.
options: In economics capital means tools, machines and buildings, not money.
Her role is to organize and take the risk, not to do the construction work.
Right: she organizes and risks her savings.
The lot is land, but she does not supply it; the town owns it.

items.q: Which country in the table has a command economy?
options: Lorna
Pavlo
Quill
Lorna and Quill together

why.correct: In a command economy the government decides what is produced, owns the businesses and sets prices.
options: Lorna leaves every decision to buyers and sellers: a market economy.
Right: planners decide, the state owns, the state sets prices.
Quill mixes markets with some government roles: a mixed economy.
Pavlo is the country that fits a command economy.

items.q: Which country in the table is closest to how most real economies work?
options: Quill, a mixed economy
Lorna, a pure market economy
Pavlo, a pure command economy
Pavlo and Lorna equally

why.correct: Most economies today rely mainly on markets but give government some roles (schools, roads, rules): mixed economies.
options: Right: markets plus some government roles.
No real economy leaves out government entirely.
Few economies plan everything centrally.
They are opposite ends; real economies sit between them.

items.q: In Lorna, how is the "for whom" question mostly answered?
options: By government planners assigning goods to each household
By giving each household the same amount
By the order in which people line up
By who is willing and able to pay market prices

why.correct: In a market economy, goods go to buyers who will pay the price, so incomes and prices decide who gets what.
options: That is how Pavlo answers it.
Equal shares are a planning choice, not a market outcome.
Prices, not lines, ration goods in a market economy.
Right: willingness and ability to pay.

items.q: In Pavlo, a factory manager is told to make 500 tractors this year. Which basic question has the government answered?
options: For whom to produce
Whether resources are scarce
What to produce
How much to charge buyers

why.correct: Setting the output of each good answers "what to produce" (and how much).
options: "For whom" is about who receives the tractors.
Scarcity is not a choice; it is why the plan is needed.
Right: the plan sets what (and how many).
Prices may also be set, but the order is about output.

items.q: Which statement about scarcity is accurate?
options: It ends once a country becomes rich enough
It exists because wants are greater than the resources to meet them
It applies to goods but not to time
It means a store has sold out of a product

why.correct: Scarcity is the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources. Rich countries and rich people face it too.
options: Wealthy societies still cannot have everything they want.
Right: limited resources, unlimited wants.
Time is one of the scarcest resources there is.
A sold-out product is a temporary market problem; scarcity is permanent.

items.q: A student has three free hours on Saturday and wants to study, work a paid shift and see friends. What does this show?
options: Scarcity: limited time forces a choice among wants
An economic system answering the question of for whom to produce
A command decision by the student's parents
A factor of production called entrepreneurship

why.correct: Time is limited and the wants are not, so the student must choose.
options: Right: a limited resource and competing wants.
Economic systems answer questions for a whole society.
Nothing says anyone else decides.
The student is not organizing a business or taking a business risk.

items.q: A city council spends this year's budget on a new bridge, so it repairs fewer school buildings. What is this an example of?
options: A command economy
An increase in resources
A choice with nothing given up
A trade-off

why.correct: Choosing more of one thing means less of another: a trade-off.
options: A city budget choice happens in every economic system.
The budget did not grow; it was divided.
School repairs were given up.
Right: the bridge comes at the cost of school repairs.

items.q: Which of these are capital in the economic sense? Select all that apply.
options: A delivery van owned by a bakery
A robot arm on a car assembly line
Cash a bakery keeps in its bank account
Crude oil still in the ground

why.correct: Capital is goods made to help produce other goods. Money is not a factor of production, and oil in the ground is land.
options: Right: a made good used to deliver bread.
Right: a machine used to build cars.
Money buys factors of production but is not one.
An unextracted natural resource is land.

items.q: Which is a service rather than a good?
options: A pair of scissors
A bottle of shampoo
A haircut
A barber's chair

why.correct: A service is an action done for someone; a good is a physical item.
options: Scissors are a good (and capital for a barber).
Shampoo is a good.
Right: the haircut is work done for you.
The chair is a good (and capital for a barber).

items.q: A country discovers a large new field of natural gas. Which factor of production has it gained more of?
options: Labor
Land
Capital
Entrepreneurship

why.correct: Natural resources count as land in economics.
options: Labor is human effort; no workers were added.
Right: natural resources are land.
Capital is made goods; the gas is natural.
Entrepreneurship is organizing and risk-taking; nothing here adds it.

items.q: A neighbor says, "Scarcity is not a problem for billionaires." What is the best reply?
options: They still face limited time and must choose how to use it and their money
They are right: with enough money each want is met
They are right, at least in a market economy
Scarcity applies to governments, not to people

why.correct: Even very rich people have limited time and face choices among wants, so scarcity applies to everyone.
options: Right: time, at least, is always limited.
Money cannot buy more hours in a day, and wants keep growing.
Scarcity does not depend on the economic system.
Every person, firm and government faces scarcity.

items.q: Put the steps from scarcity to a decision in order.
options: Wants are greater than the resources available
Resources are scarce
People must choose how to use them
Each choice gives up something else (a trade-off)

why.correct: Unlimited wants meet limited resources, which is scarcity; scarcity forces choices, and every choice is a trade-off.
